## What you'll learn

- Why a change in a strain's abundance looks like a change in expression of all of its genes.
- How **size factors** normalise samples, and why they must be computed **within each strain**.
- How to run DESeq2 with per-strain normalisation, and read volcano and MA plots.

## The problem: a strain blooms

Imagine two strains, A and B. Between two conditions, strain B becomes more abundant, and **no gene changes its expression**. Since the sequencer returns about the same number of reads either way, B's genes take a larger share of the reads and A's genes a smaller one.

A few genes in each strain truly respond (orange): A's are induced 4-fold, B's repressed 4-fold. Move the slider, and compare the normalisations.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof bloom = Inputs.range([1, 8], {value: 6, step: 0.5, label: "Strain B grows ×"})
viewof method = Inputs.radio(["Share of all reads", "Global size factors", "Per-strain size factors"], {value: "Global size factors", label: "Normalisation"})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
sim = {
  // a fixed pseudo-random community, so every learner sees the same picture
  let seed = 11;
  const rand = () => (seed = (seed * 16807) % 2147483647) / 2147483647;
  const gauss = () => Math.sqrt(-2 * Math.log(rand())) * Math.cos(2 * Math.PI * rand());
  const genes = [];
  for (const [strain, n, change] of [["A", 300, 4], ["B", 150, 1 / 4]]) {
    for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) {
      const responds = i < n / 10;
      genes.push({strain, responds, base: Math.exp(3 + 1.5 * gauss()),
                  fold: responds ? change : 1, noise1: gauss(), noise2: gauss(), jitter: rand()});
    }
  }
  return genes;
}

result = {
  const abundance = s => s === "B" ? bloom : 1;
  const c1 = sim.map(g => g.base * Math.exp(0.15 * g.noise1));
  const c2 = sim.map(g => g.base * abundance(g.strain) * g.fold * Math.exp(0.15 * g.noise2));
  // the same number of reads in both conditions
  const t1 = d3.sum(c1), t2 = d3.sum(c2);
  const lfc = sim.map((g, i) => Math.log2((c2[i] / t2) / (c1[i] / t1)));
  const shift = strains => d3.median(lfc.filter((_, i) => strains.includes(sim[i].strain)));
  const offset = {
    "Share of all reads": {A: 0, B: 0},
    "Global size factors": {A: shift(["A", "B"]), B: shift(["A", "B"])},
    "Per-strain size factors": {A: shift(["A"]), B: shift(["B"])}
  }[method];
  return sim.map((g, i) => ({...g, lfc: lfc[i] - offset[g.strain],
    status: g.responds ? "truly changed" : "unchanged"}));
}

falsePositives = result.filter(d => !d.responds && Math.abs(d.lfc) > 1).length
unchanged = result.filter(d => !d.responds).length

Plot.plot({
  height: 220, marginLeft: 70,
  x: {label: "log2 fold change", domain: [-5, 5], grid: true},
  y: {domain: [-0.5, 1.5], ticks: [0, 1], tickFormat: d => d === 1 ? "Strain A" : "Strain B", label: null},
  color: {domain: ["unchanged", "truly changed"], range: ["#8a8a8a", "#e8590c"], legend: true},
  marks: [
    Plot.ruleX([-1, 1], {stroke: "#ccc", strokeDasharray: "4,3"}),
    Plot.ruleX([0]),
    Plot.dot(result, {x: "lfc", y: d => (d.strain === "A" ? 1 : 0) + (d.jitter - 0.5) * 0.6,
                      fill: "status", r: 2.5, fillOpacity: 0.7})
  ]
})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
md`**${falsePositives} of ${unchanged}** unchanged genes have a fold change above 2 (outside the dashed lines).`
```

- **Share of all reads** (each gene's count divided by the sample's total, i.e. total-count scaling): B's genes all look induced, A's all look repressed.
- **Global size factors** (one per sample, from all genes): centre the *community* on zero. Strain A has twice as many genes as B, so the median gene, and with it the size factor, follows A: A is centred correctly, and B's genes all look induced by the full size of the bloom. Try a small bloom: global scaling can even look worse than the share of all reads, because it moves A, the majority, onto zero and leaves B off. That's the default in RNA-seq tools.
- **Per-strain size factors:** centre each strain on zero separately. Only the genes that truly changed stand out.

This is **taxon-specific scaling** ([Klingenberg & Meinicke 2017](https://doi.org/10.7717/peerj.3859)). With it, a fold change means "this gene's share of its own strain's transcripts changed", whatever happened to the strain's abundance.

In terms of the equation, transcripts = gene copies × expression: per-strain scaling removes everything that affects all of a strain's genes alike. That's the number of copies (cells), but also any change in the strain's **total** mRNA per cell. If a strain doubles the expression of every one of its genes, per-strain scaling can't see it.

## The data

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
#| edit: false
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(readr)
library(ggplot2)
suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(DESeq2))
theme_set(theme_bw())

samples <- read_csv("data/samples.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) %>%
  mutate(Treatment = factor(Treatment, levels = c("PBS", "LPS")))
genes <- read_csv("data/genes.csv.gz", show_col_types = FALSE)
counts <- read_csv("data/counts.csv.gz", show_col_types = FALSE)

# the three strains with enough reads (Part 2), as a gene x sample matrix
strains <- c("I48", "YL32", "YL58")
count_matrix <- counts %>%
  filter(locus_tag %in% genes$locus_tag[genes$genome %in% strains]) %>%
  tibble::column_to_rownames("locus_tag") %>%
  as.matrix()
storage.mode(count_matrix) <- "integer"   # DESeq2 expects whole numbers
gene_strain <- genes$genome[match(rownames(count_matrix), genes$locus_tag)]
cat(nrow(count_matrix), "genes from", length(strains), "strains in", ncol(count_matrix), "samples\n")
```

## Step 1: size factors

A **size factor** says how much more sequencing a sample got than a typical sample: divide its counts by it, and samples become comparable. DESeq2 estimates size factors with the **median of ratios**:

1. Keep genes with a count above zero in every sample, and take logs.
2. For each gene, compute its average log count over all samples: a "reference sample".
3. For each sample, compute each gene's difference to the reference (the log ratio).
4. The size factor is the exponent of the **median** log ratio over all genes.

The median makes it robust: as long as most genes don't change, the few that do don't move it.

### Exercise: median of ratios by hand

Complete step 4, then compare your function with DESeq2's.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_sizefactors
size_factors <- function(m) {
  m <- m[rowSums(m == 0) == 0, ]      # 1. genes with counts in every sample
  log_m <- log(m)
  reference <- rowMeans(log_m)        # 2. average log count of each gene
  log_ratios <- log_m - reference     # 3. each gene vs the reference
  exp(apply(log_ratios, 2, ______))   # 4. median per sample
}

i48 <- count_matrix[gene_strain == "I48", ]
round(rbind(mine = size_factors(i48), DESeq2 = estimateSizeFactorsForMatrix(i48)), 3)
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex_sizefactors"}
`apply(x, 2, f)` applies the function `f` to every column of `x`. Which function gives the median?
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex_sizefactors"}
```r
size_factors <- function(m) {
  m <- m[rowSums(m == 0) == 0, ]      # 1. genes with counts in every sample
  log_m <- log(m)
  reference <- rowMeans(log_m)        # 2. average log count of each gene
  log_ratios <- log_m - reference     # 3. each gene vs the reference
  exp(apply(log_ratios, 2, median))   # 4. median per sample
}

i48 <- count_matrix[gene_strain == "I48", ]
round(rbind(mine = size_factors(i48), DESeq2 = estimateSizeFactorsForMatrix(i48)), 3)
```
:::

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_sizefactors
#| check: true
i48 <- count_matrix[gene_strain == "I48", ]
ok <- is.function(size_factors) &&
  isTRUE(all.equal(size_factors(i48), estimateSizeFactorsForMatrix(i48)))
if (ok) {
  list(correct = TRUE, type = "success",
       message = "Your size factors are identical to DESeq2's.")
} else {
  list(correct = FALSE, type = "error",
       message = "Not yet: the size factor is exp() of the median log ratio of each sample (column).")
}
```

### Global or per strain?

Now compute size factors once for all genes together (global), and once for each strain:

```{webr}
sf <- data.frame(sample_id = colnames(count_matrix),
                 global = estimateSizeFactorsForMatrix(count_matrix))
for (s in strains) {
  sf[[s]] <- estimateSizeFactorsForMatrix(count_matrix[gene_strain == s, ])
}

sf %>%
  pivot_longer(all_of(strains), names_to = "strain", values_to = "per_strain") %>%
  left_join(samples, by = "sample_id") %>%
  ggplot(aes(global, per_strain, colour = Treatment)) +
  geom_abline(linetype = 2) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  facet_wrap(~ strain) +
  labs(x = "Global size factor", y = "Per-strain size factor")
```

If all strains kept the same proportions, each strain's points would lie on one line through the origin. They don't quite. Relative to the global size factors, I48's are on average about 15% higher in LPS mice than in PBS mice, and YL58's about 15% lower: the strains' proportions shift with treatment. Small as it is, such a shift moves **every** gene of the strain.

## Step 2: DESeq2 with per-strain size factors

DESeq2 accepts a matrix of **normalisation factors**, one per gene and sample, in place of one size factor per sample. We give every gene its own strain's size factors:

```{webr}
norm_factors <- matrix(1, nrow(count_matrix), ncol(count_matrix),
                       dimnames = dimnames(count_matrix))
for (s in strains) {
  norm_factors[gene_strain == s, ] <- matrix(sf[[s]], sum(gene_strain == s),
                                             ncol(count_matrix), byrow = TRUE)
}

coldata <- samples %>% tibble::column_to_rownames("sample_id")
dds <- DESeqDataSetFromMatrix(count_matrix, coldata[colnames(count_matrix), , drop = FALSE],
                              design = ~ Treatment)
normalizationFactors(dds) <- norm_factors
dds <- DESeq(dds, quiet = TRUE)

res <- results(dds, contrast = c("Treatment", "LPS", "PBS"), alpha = 0.01) %>%
  as.data.frame() %>%
  tibble::rownames_to_column("locus_tag") %>%
  mutate(strain = gene_strain[match(locus_tag, rownames(count_matrix))])
res %>% arrange(padj) %>% head()
```

Some genes have `NA` as their adjusted p-value. DESeq2's **independent filtering** leaves out genes whose mean count is too low to ever reach significance, which makes the multiple-testing correction less severe for the rest. The cut-off is chosen to maximise the number of significant genes at `alpha`, here 0.01. Low counts aren't the only limit: with 6 mice per group, small changes are hard to detect, and a gene that isn't significant may still respond.

::: {.callout-note}
## Why not divide the counts first?
You may find code that divides the counts by the size factors, rounds them, and gives those to DESeq2. That changes the data DESeq2 models: a count of 10 is noisier than a count of 100, and DESeq2 relies on that relationship. Normalisation factors leave the counts as they are.
:::

### What global size factors would have done

For comparison, run the same model with DESeq2's default, global size factors, and compare the fold changes of each strain:

```{webr}
dds_global <- DESeqDataSetFromMatrix(count_matrix, coldata[colnames(count_matrix), , drop = FALSE],
                                     design = ~ Treatment)
dds_global <- DESeq(dds_global, quiet = TRUE)
res_global <- results(dds_global, contrast = c("Treatment", "LPS", "PBS"), alpha = 0.01) %>%
  as.data.frame() %>%
  tibble::rownames_to_column("locus_tag") %>%
  mutate(strain = gene_strain)

bind_rows(
  data.frame(strain = gene_strain, log2FC = res$log2FoldChange, size_factors = "per strain"),
  data.frame(strain = gene_strain, log2FC = res_global$log2FoldChange, size_factors = "global")
) %>%
  ggplot(aes(log2FC, colour = size_factors)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0) +
  geom_density() +
  facet_wrap(~ strain) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(-4, 4)) +
  labs(x = "log2 fold change, LPS vs PBS", colour = "Size factors")
```

With global size factors, I48's fold changes are shifted to the right (more of its genes look induced) and YL58's to the left, as in the simulation at the top of this page. With per-strain size factors, each strain is centred on zero.

## Step 3: look at the results

A **volcano plot** shows each gene's fold change against its significance:

```{webr}
res %>%
  filter(!is.na(padj)) %>%
  mutate(call = case_when(
    padj < 0.01 & log2FoldChange > 1 ~ "up in LPS",
    padj < 0.01 & log2FoldChange < -1 ~ "down in LPS",
    TRUE ~ "not significant"
  )) %>%
  ggplot(aes(log2FoldChange, -log10(padj), colour = call)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5, size = 0.8) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(-1, 1), linetype = 2) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 2, linetype = 2) +
  facet_wrap(~ strain) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("up in LPS" = "firebrick", "down in LPS" = "steelblue",
                                 "not significant" = "grey70")) +
  labs(x = "log2 fold change, LPS vs PBS", y = "-log10 adjusted p-value", colour = NULL)
```

An **MA plot** shows fold change against mean expression. Fold changes of lowly expressed genes are noisy, so they spread widely and are rarely significant:

```{webr}
res %>%
  filter(baseMean > 0) %>%
  ggplot(aes(baseMean, log2FoldChange, colour = !is.na(padj) & padj < 0.01)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4, size = 0.6) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  facet_wrap(~ strain) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = "grey70", `TRUE` = "firebrick"),
                      labels = c("not significant", "padj < 0.01")) +
  labs(x = "Mean normalised count", y = "log2 fold change", colour = NULL)
```

### Exercise: how many genes respond?

Complete the function `count_de()` so that it counts, per strain, the genes up- and down-regulated in LPS mice at an adjusted p-value below 0.01. (Unlike the volcano plot, don't require a 2-fold change.) Then use it to compare per-strain and global size factors.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_de_summary
count_de <- function(r) {
  r %>%
    filter(!is.na(padj), ______) %>%
    group_by(strain) %>%
    summarise(up = sum(log2FoldChange > 0), down = sum(log2FoldChange < 0))
}

bind_rows(per_strain = count_de(res), global = count_de(res_global), .id = "size_factors")
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex_de_summary"}
Keep only the genes with `padj < 0.01`.
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex_de_summary"}
```r
count_de <- function(r) {
  r %>%
    filter(!is.na(padj), padj < 0.01) %>%
    group_by(strain) %>%
    summarise(up = sum(log2FoldChange > 0), down = sum(log2FoldChange < 0))
}

bind_rows(per_strain = count_de(res), global = count_de(res_global), .id = "size_factors")
```
With per-strain size factors, over 2,000 genes respond, and in every strain roughly as many go up as down. YL32 responds the most, with about 1,100 genes. With global size factors, the picture changes, most of all for I48: far fewer genes, and most of them up. That's the shift you saw in the density plot.
:::

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_de_summary
#| check: true
expected <- function(r) {
  r %>%
    filter(!is.na(padj), padj < 0.01) %>%
    group_by(strain) %>%
    summarise(up = sum(log2FoldChange > 0), down = sum(log2FoldChange < 0))
}
ok <- is.function(count_de) &&
  isTRUE(all.equal(as.data.frame(count_de(res)), as.data.frame(expected(res)))) &&
  isTRUE(all.equal(as.data.frame(count_de(res_global)), as.data.frame(expected(res_global))))
if (ok) {
  list(correct = TRUE, type = "success",
       message = "Correct. The size factors change both how many genes respond and in which direction.")
} else {
  list(correct = FALSE, type = "error",
       message = "Not yet: filter for padj < 0.01, then count positive and negative fold changes per strain.")
}
```

## Check yourself

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
import {quiz} from "../../assets/quiz.ojs"

quiz("With global size factors, 80% of strain X's genes come out as induced in the treatment. What's the most likely explanation?", [
  {text: "The treatment activates most of strain X's genes", correct: false, why: "Possible, but very unusual. A shift of almost all of a strain's genes is the signature of a change in abundance."},
  {text: "Strain X became more abundant", correct: true, why: "More cells means more transcripts of every gene. Per-strain size factors remove that shift."},
  {text: "Strain X was sequenced more deeply", correct: false, why: "Depth applies to whole samples, and global size factors already correct for it."}
])
```

## Key points

- In a community, a change in a strain's **abundance** shifts the counts of **all** its genes.
- **Size factors** normalise samples; compute them **within each strain** (taxon-specific scaling).
- Give per-strain size factors to DESeq2 as **normalisation factors**; don't divide and round the counts.
- In this experiment, thousands of genes respond to the host's inflammation, in all three strains.

Further reading: [Zhang et al. 2021](https://doi.org/10.1093/bioinformatics/btab327) compare statistical methods for differential expression in metatranscriptomes, with and without metagenomes.
